persona.who: 21, Indian-American senior at Rutgers, born in NJ. Parents from Gujarat. Dating a white classmate; hasn't told parents. Feels neither fully Indian nor American.
persona.note: my parents keep asking when I'll 'settle down with a nice Gujarati boy' and I've been with my boyfriend for 2 years and he's not Indian. I feel like whichever way I go I lose a part of me

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call being seen as less than you are, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.core_struggle: A young woman is being pressed by her parents to choose between their idea of a good match and the two-year relationship she has built with someone who is not Indian.
understanding.mirror: Two years with the person you love, and a question that asks you to lose a part of yourself no matter how you answer.
understanding.insight: The question is not which part of you to lose. It is whose picture of you you are being asked to live inside of, and why you are letting it replace your own.
understanding.mechanism_label: Being seen as less than you are

queries.hook: Being seen as less than you are by the people who raised you, and the anger of watching the life you built get called a phase. My parents' expectations weigh on me.
queries.diagnose: When others see only a role they have for you, their picture is their smallness and not your measure; the harm deepens only when their picture begins to replace your own.
queries.steady: What you are cannot be cut smaller by what they see; your worth was never theirs to grant, and standing in your own truth is itself the duty.
queries.act: Speak the true thing gently and firmly, hold your ground on what is yours, and do your own duty without shrinking to fit the picture they hold.
queries.story: A young woman of learning, dismissed by her family, who questioned them openly and stood in her truth until they had no answer.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
verse.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.
verse.why: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.
verse.misuse: Not 'stay in the role your family or birth assigned you'. It's about being true to your own nature and calling.

prasang.title: The ignorant and the wise; act free of like and dislike
prasang.summary: Krishna contrasts the attached and the wise, warns that ego claims credit for what nature does, and says to follow your own path rather than imitate another's.
prasang.lesson: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, right after Arjuna said he would rather die than fight. Arjuna is caught between his family's wishes and his own conscience, shrinking under the weight of being told who to be. Krishna tells him that living inside someone else's duty, even if they praise it, is full of fear. It is better to walk your own path, even with mistakes, than to wear a borrowed life that fits someone else's idea of perfection.
verse.for_you: The fighting with your parents is not about choosing a person. It is about refusing to wear their picture of you. Your own path, lived imperfectly, is safer than the borrowed life they are pressing you into.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: Twelve-year-old Ashtavakra is stopped at King Janaka's gate because he is 'only a boy'.
verse.sanskrit: न ज्ञायते कायवृद्ध्या विवृद्धि- / र्यथाऽष्ठीला शाल्मलेः संप्रवृद्धाः / ह्रस्वोऽल्पकायः फलितो विवृद्धो / यश्चाफलस्तस्य न वृद्धभावः
verse.line: Growth isn't size. A small tree bearing fruit has grown more than a tall, empty one.
verse.translation: Growth isn't measured by the size of the body. A short tree that bears fruit has grown; a tall one that bears none has not.
verse.why: Age and appearance don't measure wisdom. Don't dismiss anyone for being young.

prasang.title: Ashtavakra at Janaka's court
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra, born bent in eight places by his father's curse, learns at twelve that his father drowned after losing a debate to the court sage Bandi. Turned away at the gate as a child, he argues his way in and defeats Bandi.
prasang.story_hook: The gatekeeper laughed at the twelve-year-old who wanted to debate the king's greatest scholar.
prasang.lesson: Age and appearance don't measure wisdom. Don't dismiss anyone for being young.

verse.meaning: Twelve-year-old Ashtavakra, born bent in eight places, is stopped at King Janaka's gate because he is only a boy. The gatekeeper sees his small body and says he cannot enter. Ashtavakra says he is here to debate the court sage Bandi and win back his father's life. He argues that age and appearance do not measure wisdom, and that a short tree that bears fruit has grown more than a tall one that bears none. He asks the gatekeeper to let him pass, because true growth is not measured by the size of the body.
verse.for_you: Your parents keep measuring you by their own idea of a good match. That is their story, not yours. Take the seat you have already built with your partner. You do not need their approval to be whole.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Queen Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying defeated after he has lost his kingdom. She tells him not to think less of himself or settle for little. She says he must set his mind on what is truly good and stop fearing. She wants him to pull himself together and rise again.
verse.for_you: Your parents are trying to shrink you into their picture of a safe future. They are asking you to settle for less than the life you have already started building with your partner.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
verse.sanskrit: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
verse.line: You are pure awareness, wider than any worry. Don't let your mind shrink into pettiness.
verse.translation: This whole universe is pervaded by you and strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness; do not fall into smallness of mind.
verse.why: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

prasang.title: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.story_hook: A powerful king bowed before a boy whose body was bent in eight places, and asked him how to be free.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free. Ashtavakra answers that the whole universe is strung on you, and by nature you are pure awareness. The verse tells you not to fall into smallness of mind.
verse.for_you: Your parents are pressing you to shrink into their idea of a good match. You do not have to agree to be less than you are. Let their pressure land on your awareness, and let the part of you that sees the whole room stay wide and clear.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse.sanskrit: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥
verse.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.
verse.why: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.
verse.misuse: Kind speech doesn't mean avoiding hard truths; it means saying them without cruelty.

prasang.title: Three kinds of food, offering, austerity and giving
prasang.summary: Food, offering, austerity and giving each come in three kinds. Speech should be true, kind and helpful; giving should expect nothing back; effort for show doesn't last.
prasang.lesson: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.

verse.meaning: Krishna is laying out the shape of a good life. He tells Arjuna to speak words that do not hurt, that are true, that are kind, and that help. He says this is a discipline. The truth of it is that speech can either build or break a person. When you speak to build, you give someone room to breathe. When you speak to break, you shrink them. This is the standard. It asks for a kind of attention to the words you choose, so they do not become weapons.
verse.for_you: The words your parents use to describe your future are taking up space. Speak one true, kind and helpful sentence to yourself today. Name the person you are becoming, not the picture they want to hang.

verse.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
verse.setting: Brihaspati counsels Indra on how to hold authority among difficult people.
verse.sanskrit: मृदुमप्यवमन्यन्ते तीक्ष्णादुद्विजते जनः / मातीक्ष्णो मा मृदुर्भूस्त्वं तीक्ष्णो भव मृदुर्भव
verse.line: People walk over the soft and fear the harsh. Be firm when it's needed, gentle when it's needed.
verse.translation: People look down even on the gentle, and they shrink from the harsh. Do not be only harsh, do not be only soft: be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is.
verse.misuse: Firmness here means clarity, not cruelty.

verse.meaning: Brihaspati tells Indra that people walk over the soft and fear the harsh. This is a warning about how the world treats a ruler who cannot set a boundary. The verse says do not be only harsh, do not be only soft. Be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is.
verse.for_you: Your parents are shrinking you because they see only their own fear. You do not have to match their harshness to be heard. You need a clear line, spoken without cruelty, that holds the shape of your life.

story.title: Kausalya lets Ram go
story.story_hook: His mother had waited seventeen years for this day, and it was taken from her in a morning.
story.summary: Ram's mother faints at the news and begs to come with him. Ram gently refuses, asks her to look after his grieving father, and wins her blessing for the journey.
story.lesson: Love sometimes means staying behind to care for someone else.

anchor.speaker: Ram
anchor.setting: Ram's mother wants to follow him into exile; he asks her instead to stay and look after his grieving father.
anchor.sanskrit: यथा मयि तु निष्क्रान्ते पुत्रशोकेन पार्थिवः॥ श्रमं नावाप्नुयात् किंचिदप्रमत्ता तथा कुरु। दारुणश्चाप्ययं शोको यथैनं न विनाशयेत्॥ राज्ञो वृद्धस्य सततं हितं चर समाहिता।
anchor.line: When I'm gone, look after him. Don't let his grief wear him down.
anchor.translation: Take care that when I am gone the king does not wear himself out with grief for his son, that this terrible sorrow does not destroy him. Look after the old king's welfare always.
anchor.why: Love sometimes means staying behind to care for someone else.

prasang.title: Kausalya lets Ram go
prasang.summary: Ram's mother faints at the news and begs to come with him. Ram gently refuses, asks her to look after his grieving father, and wins her blessing for the journey.
prasang.story_hook: His mother had waited seventeen years for this day, and it was taken from her in a morning.
prasang.lesson: Love sometimes means staying behind to care for someone else.

story.hook_title: Kausalya waited years for Ram's crowning, and lost him in a morning
story.teaser: Kausalya waited years for Ram's crowning, and lost him in a morning
story.for_you: Kausalya let Ram go because she saw his path and chose to hold the ground she stood on. You are being asked to leave your path too. But the question is not whether to go. It is whether you will step aside so your parents can hold the ground they are standing on.

script: You are shrinking. You feel pulled apart, and every choice feels like a loss. The fighting with your parents is loud, and you are caught in the middle of it.
Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He has just said he would rather die than fight his own family. He is trapped between his duty to his kin and what his own conscience demands. And Krishna replies:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्, स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः.
In plain words: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.

Krishna tells him that living inside someone else's duty, even done perfectly, is full of fear. Borrowed lives are dangerous because they are not yours. It is better to walk your own path, even if you stumble. This is easier said than done, because your family is pressing you to fit their picture of a good life. But the truth underneath is that you cannot breathe in a shape that was cut for someone else.

The fighting with your parents is not about choosing a person. It is about refusing to wear their picture of you. Your own path, lived imperfectly, is safer than the borrowed life they are pressing you into.
Whose picture of you will you step out of today?

depth.life: You are on the phone, scrolling, trying to shrink yourself. Your parents want you to become someone else, to live inside their picture of you. You keep fighting, but the pressure is on you to choose their life. You feel torn because you are being asked to disappear.
depth.points: The texts say a borrowed life is full of fear. Your parents are offering you a role that is not yours. To take it is to wear a mask that does not fit, and that is where the danger lives, not in your own imperfect steps.
depth.practice: Put the phone down for ten minutes and sit with your own thoughts. Do not call or message anyone. Just let your mind be quiet.
depth.question: What would you do if you were not trying to please anyone?
